name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I do the marketing at Harrow & Sons, a family biscuit maker that's been baking shortbread in this town for ninety years. I write what goes on the tins and packets, plan the Christmas campaign, which is half our year, and run our stand at the county shows. I sit in an office above the bakery, so the whole place smells of butter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that it's a proper family firm. Old Mr Harrow still walks round at eleven every day and knows everyone's name. What wears me down is the pay, which is low, and the fact that I'm getting married next September to Ruth, my fiancée, with about three weeks' money saved. His son, young Mr Harrow, is taking over next year, and he keeps saying the word modernise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. A machine has never tasted shortbread, so I don't see the point of it writing about shortbread. Young Mr Harrow has mentioned it, and I've nodded and carried on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad if it all blew over, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my granddad would have said: there's no substitute for hard work and knowing your trade. I'd say it at church and at the pub. I wouldn't bother posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still worried, just not about computers. Young Mr Harrow wants to modernise, and I'm not sure where I fit in that. And the wedding's going to cost more than we've got, however we cut it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, and make sure this Christmas campaign is the best one yet. Ruth and I would cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty and have the do in the church hall. I'd put whatever I can, maybe thirty a week, into a savings jar for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's the wedding and the new boss, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would modernise mean, at Harrow & Sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Mr Harrow went to business school, and he talks about selling online and cutting costs. To me, a tin of shortbread is about trust, not clicks. I'm worried he'll want someone younger with the shiny tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did Ruth take the idea of cutting the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than I did. Ruth said she'd rather have a small wedding than start married life in debt. Her mum was less happy, but she came round.

say: I'd say there's **no substitute** for hard work and knowing your trade.
I'd say it at **church** and the pub, not online.
think: I think the risk is the **new boss**, not computers.
The **wedding** will cost more than we've got.
do: Make this **Christmas campaign** the best one yet.
Cut the **guest list** from a hundred to sixty.
Save **thirty a week** in a jar for the wedding.
feel: I feel **worried**, by the wedding costs and the new boss more than machines.
S0.quote: To me, a tin of shortbread is about trust, not clicks.
fieldNote: His worry comes from a **change of owner** and a wedding, not AI.
He sees trust and **tradition** as his defence.
His fiancée is the more **practical** one about money.

steps.text: Make this year's Harrow & Sons Christmas campaign the best yet
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty
Put thirty a week into a wedding savings jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and planning. That's what young Mr Harrow would grab first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should look after the people who've been loyal to them. I'd say it's not the government's job to fix everything, but it's the firm's job not to throw people away. At church I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the one who goes. Young Mr Harrow would buy the AI, have it write the tins and plan the Christmas campaign, and keep one person who knows how to use it. That person isn't me, because I've dug my heels in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about working on his roofing crew, just in case. I'd keep doing my job and hope young Mr Harrow sees what the old ways are worth, at least for the first months. And Ruth and I would ask her parents whether we could live with them for the first year after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like I've chosen the wrong side and I'm too proud to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said too proud to switch. Would you learn the tool if it saved your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if it came to that, and I'd hate every minute. But I'd still rather put my hands to work than sit there pressing a button to make a machine write about biscuits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad take you asking about roofing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I told you so. He always wanted me on the crew instead of going to university. He'd have me up a ladder by Monday.

say: I'd say firms should **look after** loyal people.
I'd say it's the firm's job, not **government's**, to do right by staff.
think: I think I'm **the one who goes**, because I refused the tools.
Young Mr Harrow would keep **one person** who uses AI.
do: Ask my dad about a place on his **roofing crew**.
Keep doing my job and hope the **old ways** count.
Ask Ruth's parents if we can **live with them** after the wedding.
feel: I feel **sick**, like I chose the **wrong side**.
S1.quote: I'd still rather put my hands to work than sit there pressing a button to make a machine write about biscuits.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** and knows his stubbornness adds to the risk.
His backstop is **family**: his dad's crew and his fiancée's parents.
He blames the **firm**, not the government, if loyalty isn't rewarded.

steps.text: Keep writing the tins by hand and wait for young Mr Harrow's move
Ask his dad about a place on the roofing crew
Ask Ruth's parents if the couple can live with them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our first anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to lean on their families and their churches, because nobody else is ready. I'd say firms owe their people notice and a decent send-off. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, but I'd want apprenticeships, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm out at Harrow & Sons by 2028, maybe sooner. The thinking side goes first, and that's all I do. Robots won't be up on roofs until about 2031, so my dad's crew gives me three years, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad and start on the roofing crew as soon as I could, even before I lost the office job, at weekends. Ruth and I would scale the wedding right down, just the church and family, and move in with her parents. I'd ask the church about anyone who needs work doing, to bring in extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. But I'd know where to go, which is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth the night it became real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not going under, because we've got family. Then I'd probably go quiet for a bit. She'd make tea and tell me to stop being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Roofing is hard, physical work. Are you ready for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did summers on the crew as a lad, so I know what it's like. My back will complain. But a sore back is better than an empty bank account.

say: I'd say people should lean on **families and churches**.
I'd ask for **apprenticeships**, not handouts, and decent notice from firms.
think: I think I'm **out** at Harrow & Sons by 2028.
My dad's **roofing crew** gives me three years before robots, around 2031.
do: Start on the **roofing crew** at weekends, then full-time.
Scale the wedding to **church and family** and move in with Ruth's parents.
Ask the church about **odd jobs** for extra cash.
feel: I feel **scared**, but I'd know **where to go**.
S2.quote: A sore back is better than an empty bank account.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** fast and turns straight to his father's trade.
**Family and church** are his safety net, not the state.
The wedding becomes **smaller**, but he won't cancel it.

steps.text: Start on his dad's roofing crew at weekends
Hold a small church wedding with family only
Move in with Ruth's parents after the wedding
Take odd jobs from people at church for extra cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, there's a bit of room in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when young people should be getting into trades, and firms should be offering apprenticeships. I'd tell the lads at church to think hard about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I still lose the office job around 2031. But with five years, I could do a proper roofing apprenticeship and be qualified before then. Robots don't come for roofs until about 2034. Old slate roofs round here will take the robots longer than anything in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Harrow & Sons for now and do the wedding as planned, but smaller. I'd start a roofing course at the college next autumn, evenings, while helping my dad on Saturdays. I'd save toward my own tools and a van, maybe forty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. I'd be building something I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the county shows, chatting to people about our tins. But I never loved the office part. Maybe the trade suits me more than I wanted to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would old Mr Harrow say, if you left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd shake my hand and say good lad. He started as a baker's boy himself. It's young Mr Harrow who wouldn't notice.

say: I'd say young people should get into **trades**.
I'd tell the lads at church to think hard about **apprenticeships** while there's time.
think: I think I **still lose** the office job around 2031.
With five years I could be a **qualified roofer** before robots, around 2034.
do: Start a **roofing course** at college next autumn, in the evenings.
Save **forty a week** toward tools and a van.
feel: I feel **worried, but steadier**, building something I can see.
S3.quote: Old slate roofs round here will take the robots longer than anything in an office.
fieldNote: The extra time turns a scramble into a **proper apprenticeship**.
He admits the **trade** may suit him more than the office.
He values **old Mr Harrow's** blessing over the son's opinion.

steps.text: Start an evening roofing course at the college next autumn
Save forty a week toward his own tools and van
Stay at Harrow & Sons and help his dad on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. I'd have kids by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do things properly: apprenticeships, families looking after their own, firms giving notice. I wouldn't want the government taking it all over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in marketing too long, knowing me. It's still the end point, but ten years feels far off, and I'm not one to move before I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned and try to stay at Harrow & Sons. I'd help my dad at weekends and pick up the roofing skills slowly. I'd vote for whoever puts money into apprenticeships. And I'd start saving for a house, not just the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It's far enough off that I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay too long. What would make you move in time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, probably, or the first baby. If I had a child to feed, I wouldn't wait for my boss to decide for me. I'd go to my dad's crew and get qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would let you stay in marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people still wanted a real person behind a family firm's name, maybe. I think some will. I just don't think there'll be enough of them to pay a wage.

say: I'd say there's time for **apprenticeships** and families looking after their own.
I wouldn't want the **government** taking it all over.
think: I think I'd **stay too long** in marketing, knowing me.
Ten years feels **far off**, so I'd move only when I must.
do: Go ahead with **the wedding** and save for a house.
Help my dad at **weekends** to learn roofing slowly.
S4.quote: If I had a child to feed, I wouldn't wait for my boss to decide for me.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him **keep life plans** but invites delay.
A **first child** is what he says would push him to move.
He doubts enough people will pay for a **human touch**.

steps.text: Hold the wedding as planned and save for a house
Stay at Harrow & Sons and learn roofing at weekends
Vote for parties that fund apprenticeships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It hits right as Ruth and I start married life with nothing saved. Quick, paid apprenticeships in proper trades would let men like me earn while we learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It's what keeps me steady when I can't see the way. People laugh at that, but it's real.

headlineQuote: Quick, paid apprenticeships in proper trades would let men like me earn while we learn.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old marketer** at a ninety-year-old family biscuit firm, on low pay.
He's getting **married next September** with about three weeks saved.
He has **never used AI** and leans on family, church and trades, not the state.
He's **anxious** in the calm picture and **alarmed** when AI moves fast.
His fallback is his dad's **roofing crew**, which he once turned down.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as he starts married life with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in proper trades, so he can earn while he learns.
